lead: CompTIA's entry-level project management cert. It proves you can run a small or medium IT project from start to finish: scope, schedule, budget, risk, change control and communication, in both waterfall and agile. Useful the first time you're put in charge of a cutover, a hardware refresh or a new system.
objSub: Four domains and 24 objectives from CompTIA's PK0-005 objectives. Tick objectives as you study; progress saves on this device.

v5.label: V5
v5.note: The only version on sale. CompTIA hasn't announced a retirement date or a new version yet. It says exams usually retire about three years after launch, so check the exam page before you buy a voucher.
v5.onote: Official CompTIA objectives (PK0-005), in plain words. Domain weights are from CompTIA's exam page.

domains.name: Project Management Concepts
obj: Project characteristics, methodologies and frameworks
Projects are temporary and unique, with a start and finish; programs and portfolios; waterfall, Scrum, Kanban, XP, SAFe, PRINCE2, DevOps, DevSecOps and the SDLC.
Agile vs waterfall
Choosing by tolerance for change, how clear the requirements are, budget and schedule; team makeup and roles; how communication differs.
Change control
Log and review change requests, assess the impact, take them to the decision maker or change control board, update the plan, then validate and communicate. Product vs project change; scope creep.
Risk management
Known and unknown risks; qualitative vs quantitative analysis; responses to threats (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) and opportunities (exploit, enhance, share, accept); risk owners.
Issue management
Issue logs, owners and escalation paths; root cause analysis, contingency plans and workarounds; documenting the outcome.
Schedule development and management
Milestones, activities and sprint goals; dependencies like finish-to-start; estimates, story points and buffers; critical path; revise the baseline vs rebaseline.
Quality and performance management
Retrospectives and lessons learned; SLAs, KPIs and OKRs; cost and schedule variance; audits; unit, smoke, regression, stress and user acceptance testing.
Communication management
Synchronous vs asynchronous, formal vs informal, internal vs external; time zones and language; keeping records; revising the communication plan.
Meeting management
Workshops, stand-ups, demos, status and steering meetings; agendas, timeboxing, facilitator and scribe; minutes and action items.
Team and resource management
Functional, matrix and projectized organizations; resource gaps; forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning; sponsor, product owner, Scrum master, SMEs.
Procurement and vendor selection
Build, buy, lease or subscribe; RFI, RFQ, RFP and RFB; best value vs lowest cost; fixed price, time and materials, cost plus; MSA, SOW, PO and NDA.

domains.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
obj: Discovery and concept artifacts
Business case and ROI, current vs future state, prequalified vendors and existing contracts, SOWs, CapEx vs OpEx.
Initiation
Project charter with objectives, success criteria and preliminary scope; stakeholders; a RACI matrix; access requirements; the kickoff meeting.
Planning
Assign resources; communication plan, scope statement, WBS or backlog, schedule, budget, quality plan, risk assessment, transition and release plans; baselines.
Execution
Work the plan; organizational change (training, adoption); manage vendors; track progress, budget and timeline; resolve conflict; phase gate reviews.
Closing
Validate deliverables, close contracts, remove access, release resources, write the closeout report, archive documents, reconcile the budget, get sign-off.

domains.name: Tools and Documentation
obj: Project tools
Gantt, burndown, PERT and network diagrams, milestone charts; issue, defect and change logs; risk register; status reports, dashboards, task boards and a requirements traceability matrix.
Productivity tools
Communication, collaboration, meeting, office, scheduling and ticketing tools, in the cloud or on premises.
Quality and performance charts
Histograms, Pareto, run, control and scatter charts, fishbone diagrams, burnup and burndown, velocity charts and decision trees.

domains.name: Basics of IT and Governance
obj: ESG factors
A project's effect on the environment, regulations and standards, company values and brand.
Information security
Physical (devices, media, facility access), operational (screening, clearances), digital (permissions, remote access, MFA) and data security (classification, need to know).
Compliance and privacy
PII and PHI, legal and regulatory requirements, privacy laws by country and state, industry rules.
IT concepts
Infrastructure (compute, multitier, networking, storage), IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, and enterprise software like ERP, CRM and databases.
Operational change control
Maintenance windows, user notifications, rollback plans and validation checks; software change approval and testing; CI/CD; production vs staging.

extras.title: Risk responses
rows: Change the plan so the risk can't happen
Lower the chance or the impact
Shift the impact to someone else: insurance, contract, vendor
Do nothing now; keep a contingency ready
Raise the chance or the benefit
Team up with someone who can help capture it

extras.title: Change control
rows: Receive the change request and log it.
Assess the impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality and risk.
Recommend a decision and take it to the decision maker or change control board.
If approved, update the plan and baselines.
Implement the change and validate it.
Tell stakeholders the result and close the request.

extras.title: Documents by phase
rows: Why do it: costs, ROI, current vs future state
Authorizes the project and names the PM
Who's Responsible, Accountable (only one), Consulted, Informed
Breaks the scope into work packages you can estimate
Every risk, its owner, its response
Every change request and its decision

extras.title: Schedule and cost math
rows: Zero float. Any slip delays the whole project
How long a task can slip without delaying the end

method: Use the four domains above as your checklist. Domains 1.0 and 2.0 are almost two-thirds of the exam.
Pick one book or video course and finish it. Learn the vocabulary exactly: CompTIA's answers turn on the right term.
Run a real small project at your unit, or plan a pretend one: write a charter, a WBS, a RACI, a Gantt chart and a risk register.
Flashcards for risk responses, documents by phase, chart types, contract types and the change control steps.
Timed practice exams. Review every miss, especially the “what should the PM do FIRST” questions.
tips: When a stakeholder asks for a change, the answer is almost never “just do it.” It goes through change control.
Many questions are really asking which phase you're in. Name the phase first, then pick the action.
FIRST, BEST and NEXT change the answer. Several options can be true; only one fits the qualifier.
Performance-based questions can eat time. Flag them, finish the multiple choice, then come back.

quiz.q: A server cutover is scheduled for the same week as an exercise that could pull your key techs away. The PM moves the cutover two weeks later so the conflict can't happen. Which risk response is this?
o: Avoid
Right. Changing the plan so the risk can no longer occur is avoidance.
Mitigate
Mitigation lowers the chance or impact, like cross-training a backup tech. Here the risk is removed entirely.
Transfer
Transfer shifts the impact to a third party, like a contract or insurance.
Accept
Accepting means keeping the date and living with the risk.

quiz.q: A new contract vehicle would cut hardware costs 20% if the order is placed before month end. The PM assigns a buyer full time to make sure it's placed in time. Which response is this?
o: Exploit
Right. Exploit means acting to make sure a positive risk (an opportunity) actually happens.
Enhance
Enhance raises the chance or size of the benefit without making it certain.
Share
Share means teaming up with another party to capture the opportunity.
Mitigate
Mitigate is a response to threats, not opportunities.

quiz.q: Midway through a project, a division chief asks one of your techs directly to add a new reporting feature. What should happen FIRST?
o: Submit a change request so it's logged and its impact is assessed
Right. Every change goes through change control: log it, assess scope, schedule, cost and risk, then get a decision.
Add it if the tech says it's small
That's scope creep. Small unplanned changes add up and nobody approved them.
Update the schedule baseline to include it
The baseline changes only after a change is approved.
Have the sponsor approve it right away
The decision maker needs the impact analysis first. Approval comes after assessment.

quiz.q: Task A (3 days) starts the project. Tasks B (5 days) and C (2 days) both follow A. Task D (4 days) follows C. Task E (2 days) follows both B and D. What is the project's length, and which task has float?
o: 11 days; task B has 1 day of float
Right. A-C-D-E = 3+2+4+2 = 11 days is the critical path. A-B-E = 10 days, so B can slip 1 day.
10 days; task C has 1 day of float
A-B-E is 10 days, but the longest path sets the length. A-C-D-E is 11, and C is on it.
11 days; no task has float
B isn't on the critical path, so it has float.
16 days; every task is critical
You don't add every task: B and the C-D chain run at the same time.

quiz.q: Two weeks into a project, team members argue over roles and push back on the PM's decisions. Which stage of team development is this?
o: Storming
Right. Conflict over roles and authority is storming. The PM helps the team work through it.
Forming
Forming is the polite, getting-to-know-you start.
Norming
In norming the team has settled its roles and works together.
Adjourning
Adjourning is when the project ends and the team breaks up.

quiz.q: A unit is replacing on-premises email with a cloud suite. A policy fixes the requirements, the contract has a firm delivery date, and users can't test until cutover. Which approach fits BEST?
o: Waterfall
Right. Fixed requirements, a fixed date and one big delivery with no chance for frequent user feedback suit a predictive, phase-by-phase plan.
Scrum
Scrum fits changing requirements and users who can review working pieces every sprint.
Kanban
Kanban suits a steady flow of ongoing work, like a help desk queue.
Extreme Programming (XP)
XP is a set of software development practices, not a fit for a fixed service migration.

quiz.q: Which document formally authorizes a project, names the project manager and states its high-level objectives?
o: Project charter
Right. The charter is the initiation document that gives the PM authority to use resources.
Statement of work (SOW)
A SOW describes the work a vendor or team will deliver. It doesn't authorize the project.
Business case
The business case justifies the project in discovery, before it's authorized.
Project management plan
That's built during planning, after the charter.

quiz.q: In a draft RACI for a network refresh, three techs, the PM and the division chief are all marked A on the cutover task. What's wrong?
o: Each task should have exactly one Accountable person
Right. Many people can be Responsible, but one person is Accountable so there's no confusion over who owns the result.
Everyone doing the work should be marked A
People doing the work are Responsible (R).
Every task needs at least one Informed person
Not required, and it doesn't fix the problem of five owners.
Consulted and Informed should be merged
C (asked before) and I (told after) are different on purpose.

quiz.q: The customer has accepted the deliverables. Which of these is a CLOSING activity?
o: Remove project access, release resources and archive the documents
Right. Closing also includes closing contracts, the closeout report, lessons learned and sign-off.
Hold the kickoff meeting
Kickoff is at the end of initiation.
Add newly found risks to the risk register
That's ongoing risk work during planning and execution.
Run a phase gate review before the next phase
Phase gates sit between phases during execution.

quiz.q: Leadership would rather pay monthly for a cloud service than buy servers up front. In budget terms, the project is shifting from:
o: CapEx to OpEx
Right. Buying servers is a capital expense; a monthly subscription is an operating expense.
OpEx to CapEx
That's backwards. Up-front purchases are capital expenses.
Fixed price to time and materials
Those are contract types, not budget categories.
ROI to TCO
Those are ways to evaluate cost and value, not types of expense.

quiz.q: The help desk logged 400 outage tickets by cause. You want to show leadership the few causes behind most of the tickets so the team fixes those first. Which chart?
o: Pareto chart
Right. Bars sorted from most to least, plus a cumulative line, show the vital few causes (the 80/20 rule).
Histogram
A histogram shows a distribution but isn't sorted to highlight the top causes.
Fishbone diagram
A fishbone brainstorms the possible causes of ONE problem. It doesn't count tickets.
Scatter diagram
A scatter diagram shows whether two variables are related.

quiz.q: On a 10-day sprint burndown chart, the remaining-work line stays flat for days 1 to 4, then drops steeply. What does it MOST likely show?
o: Work wasn't being completed early on, so the sprint goal is at risk. Look for blockers
Right. A flat line means nothing is being finished. A late cliff often means rushed work or late updates.
The team is ahead of schedule
Ahead would put the line below the ideal line early, not flat.
Work was added to the sprint
Added scope makes the line go UP, not stay flat.
Velocity went up for the next sprint
One sprint's shape doesn't set the next sprint's velocity.

quiz.q: A security patch must go to production servers. Which plan BEST follows operational change control?
o: Test it in staging, schedule it in an approved maintenance window, notify users and keep a rollback plan
Right. Testing, approval, notification, a window and a way back are the core of IT change control.
Install it in production during business hours so the team can watch it
Untested changes during peak hours put users at risk and skip approval.
Try it on one production server first, without approval
Production isn't a test bed, and skipping approval breaks change control.
Skip the notice because patching is routine
Users still need to know about outages and reboots.

quiz.q: A vendor needs a list of users to create accounts. Your spreadsheet has names, SSNs, home addresses and duty phone numbers. What should the PM do?
o: Send only the fields the vendor needs, through an approved encrypted channel, after confirming the contract covers handling PII
Right. Need to know and data minimization: share the least data, securely, under an agreement.
Email the whole spreadsheet, since the vendor signed an NDA
An NDA doesn't make it OK to share SSNs and addresses the vendor doesn't need.
Post it to the team's shared site so the vendor can download it
That exposes PII to everyone with access to the site.
Refuse to give the vendor any data
The project still needs accounts. The answer is minimum data, shared safely.

pbqs.title: Name the phase and the document
pbqs.scenario: You're running a network refresh for your unit. For each moment, pick the phase you're in and the document you'd use.

rows.req: Leadership wants to know why the refresh is worth funding: costs, ROI, and today vs after.
rows.why: The business case justifies the project during discovery, before it's approved.

rows.req: The commanding officer formally approves the project and names you project manager.
rows.why: The charter authorizes the project and the PM. It's the key initiation document.

rows.req: Decide who does, who owns, who's asked and who's told for each task.
rows.why: The RACI is built in initiation, alongside identifying stakeholders.

rows.req: Break the scope into small work packages the team can estimate.
rows.why: The work breakdown structure is a planning document.

rows.req: The switches arrive damaged. You record it, assign an owner and track it to resolution.
rows.why: A problem happening now is an issue, tracked in the issue log during execution.

rows.req: Record the results, the lessons learned and the sign-off.
rows.why: The closeout report wraps up the project.

pbqs.title: Pick the risk response
pbqs.scenario: Each line is a decision you made on a project. Pick the risk response. Each answer is used once; one is a distractor.

items.text: Your only firewall expert might transfer mid-project. You pair a second tech with them now so the knowledge isn't lost.
items.why: Mitigate: you can't stop the transfer, but you lower its impact.

items.text: Migrating an unsupported old system could break the cutover, so you drop it from scope.
items.why: Avoid: changing the scope removes the risk entirely.

items.text: The contract makes the vendor pay for any delay their late hardware causes.
items.why: Transfer: the financial impact shifts to the vendor through the contract.

items.text: There's a small chance the training room projector fails. You decide to live with it.
items.why: Accept: the impact is low, so you take no action now.

items.text: A sister unit is buying the same licenses. You combine the orders so both units get the volume discount.
items.why: Share: you team up with another party to capture an opportunity.

items.text: Finishing early would let your unit join a pilot program. You add a second shift to raise the odds.
items.why: Enhance: you raise the chance of the good outcome without guaranteeing it.

pbqs.title: Choose the chart
pbqs.scenario: Each request came from your sponsor. Pick the chart or tool that answers it. Each answer is used once; two are distractors.

items.text: Show every task on a timeline with its dates and dependencies.
items.why: A Gantt chart shows tasks as bars over time, with dependencies.

items.text: Show how much sprint work is left each day compared with the ideal pace.
items.why: A burndown chart tracks remaining work against an ideal line.

items.text: Find the few causes behind most of the outage tickets.
items.why: A Pareto chart sorts causes by count with a cumulative line.

items.text: Brainstorm every possible cause of slow logins, grouped by people, process and technology.
items.why: A fishbone (cause and effect) diagram groups possible causes of one problem.

items.text: Check whether more users online means longer page load times.
items.why: A scatter diagram shows whether two variables move together.

items.text: Compare the expected value of buying vs leasing, with the chances of each outcome.
items.why: A decision tree weighs options by probability and value.

keep.text: Earned on or after Oct 1, 2025: renew every 3 years with 30 continuing education units (CEUs) and the CE fee, or by passing the current Project+ exam again.
keep.after: Earned by Sep 30, 2025: it's good for life. CompTIA also gave those holders a Project+ ce version they can keep active (first deadline Oct 1, 2028). Renewing Project+ doesn't renew any other CompTIA cert.

keep.text: Project+ isn't on the DoD 8140 matrix. For the IT Project Manager (802) and Program Manager (801) work roles, CompTIA lists Security+ and SecurityX as the approved certs.
keep.after: If you're filling a coded project billet, get Security+ first. Project+ adds the project skills on top.

keep.text: Good for anyone who leads cutovers, refreshes or installs. Use CG COOL for the voucher.
keep.after: If you go civilian, it's a first step toward PMI's CAPM and PMP.
